SENIOR BACKEND ENGINEER, PAYMENTS & LEDGER
Tallowmarket, Inc. | Denver, CO

ABOUT TALLOWMARKET
Tallowmarket is a B2B marketplace where independent restaurants buy directly from regional farms and ranches. Our Payments & Ledger group moves about $1.1B a year through escrowed payouts to more than 6,500 growers. We are a team of 140 people, about 55 of them in engineering. Our backend is Go on PostgreSQL, with Kafka between services and Temporal for long-running payment workflows.

WHAT YOU WILL DO
- Own services in the money path: escrow holds, split payouts to growers, refunds and chargebacks.
- Design and evolve Harrow, our double-entry ledger built on PostgreSQL, as volume grows from 400,000 to a projected 1.5 million ledger entries per day.
- Improve the reliability of the nightly settlement batch that runs at 02:00 Mountain Time and must finish before banks open.
- Lead technical design reviews and mentor mid-level engineers on the team.
- Join the on-call rotation, currently one week in six.
- Partner with Finance and Risk on reconciliation and audit requirements.

WHAT YOU BRING
- 5+ years of professional backend experience in Go, Java or Kotlin.
- Deep PostgreSQL knowledge: indexing, locking, isolation levels, and safe online migrations.
- Experience with event-driven systems (Kafka, Kinesis or similar) and idempotent processing.
- A track record of leading multi-engineer projects from design doc to launch.
- Clear written communication; we make most decisions in design docs.

NICE TO HAVE
- Prior work on a double-entry ledger or a payments platform.
- Experience reducing PCI DSS scope.
- Stripe Connect or Adyen for Platforms integration experience.
- Experience with Temporal or another durable workflow engine.

COMPENSATION
Base salary band: $172,000 - $208,000 USD, plus equity and a 6% 401(k) match. This role is leveled at L5 (Senior).

INTERVIEW PROCESS
Recruiter screen (30 minutes), a 60-minute ledger design exercise, a Go coding session, and a values conversation with our Director of Engineering, Imani Castellanos.

Tallowmarket is an equal opportunity employer.

SALES-CTX-G1.title: Trellis Flow one-pager and pricing and packaging sheet (rev 4.1)
SALES-CTX-G1.text:
CORVANE SYSTEMS - TRELLIS FLOW
Product one-pager and pricing and packaging sheet, revision 4.1, effective 1 September 2026.

WHAT IT IS
Trellis Flow automates accounts payable for mid-market finance teams. It captures vendor invoices from email, PDF upload or EDI, extracts the fields, matches them against purchase orders and receipts, routes exceptions for approval, and posts approved bills to the ERP. Target customer: 100 to 2,000 employees, 1,500 to 40,000 invoices a month, finance team of 3 to 25 people.

HEADLINE RESULTS
Customer-reported medians across 41 customers live for at least six months. Corvane has not independently audited these figures.
- Cost per processed invoice down 63 percent (from $11.40 to about $4.20)
- Approval cycle time down from 4.1 days to 1.6 days
- Touchless rate (invoices posted with no human touch) 71 percent at month six
Customer references are available only after a mutual NDA is signed. Corvane does not publish customer names.

PLANS (monthly list price, billed annually in advance)
Starter: $1,900 a month. Up to 2,000 invoices a month, 1 entity, 10 users, QuickBooks Online and Xero connectors, email support, 99.5 percent uptime target. No SSO.
Growth: $4,800 a month. Up to 10,000 invoices a month, up to 3 entities, 40 users, NetSuite and QuickBooks Online connectors, Dynamics 365 Business Central connector (beta), SAML SSO, two-way and three-way matching, 99.9 percent uptime SLA, business-hours support with 4-hour first response.
Enterprise: from $14,500 a month, quoted per deal. More than 10,000 invoices a month, unlimited entities, SAP S/4HANA connector (generally available), SCIM provisioning, EU data residency (Frankfurt), 99.95 percent uptime SLA, named customer success manager, 24x7 support with 1-hour first response for severity 1 issues.
Overage: $0.85 per invoice above the plan limit on Starter and Growth. Enterprise overage is set in the order form.

IMPLEMENTATION (one-time fee)
Starter: self-serve, $0. Growth: $12,000 fixed fee, typically 6 weeks from kickoff to go-live. Enterprise: from $38,000, typically 10 to 14 weeks. Data migration (vendor master, open purchase orders, historical bills by CSV or API) takes 5 to 7 business days and is included in the fee. A Workday Financials connector is on the roadmap for Q2 2027 and is not a commitment.

DISCOUNTS AND COMMERCIAL TERMS
- Annual prepay is the list price basis. Monthly billing costs 10 percent more.
- Multi-year: 2-year term 10 percent off, 3-year term 15 percent off, applied to subscription only, never to implementation fees.
- Sales reps may approve up to 10 percent total discount. Anything above 10 percent needs Deal Desk approval. Discounts above 20 percent are not offered.
- Standard payment terms are net 30. Net 45 needs Deal Desk approval. Net 60 is not offered. Quarterly billing is available on Growth and Enterprise with a 3 percent surcharge.
- Default term is 12 months, auto-renews for 12 months, 60 days' written notice to cancel. Renewal increases are capped at 5 percent.
- No termination for convenience. Termination for cause with a 30-day cure period.
- Corvane liability is capped at 12 months of fees. Uncapped liability is not offered. On Enterprise only, a data breach super-cap of 2x annual fees is negotiable.

PROOF OF VALUE
There is no self-serve free trial. Qualified Growth and Enterprise prospects can run a 30-day proof of value in a sandbox using up to 500 of their own historical invoices at no charge. It requires a signed evaluation agreement and one named technical contact.

SECURITY AND COMPLIANCE
SOC 2 Type II (most recent report period ended 31 March 2026). ISO 27001 certification is in progress with a target of Q1 2027; Corvane is not yet certified. AES-256 encryption at rest, TLS 1.2 or higher in transit. Data is hosted in the US by default; EU residency (Frankfurt) is Enterprise only. Annual third-party penetration test, summary available under NDA. No security incident requiring customer notification since launch in 2021.

SALES-CTX-G2.title: Trellis Flow competitive battlecard and field FAQ
SALES-CTX-G2.text:
TRELLIS FLOW - COMPETITIVE BATTLECARD AND FIELD FAQ
Corvane Systems sales enablement. Updated 12 August 2026. Internal use only.

READ THIS FIRST
Competitor information comes from win/loss calls, public web pages and what prospects tell us. It can be wrong or out of date. Never quote a competitor's price or security status to a prospect as fact. Say what we know about ourselves and suggest the prospect asks the competitor directly.

PAYLANE
Typical quote reported by prospects for around 10,000 invoices a month: $3,100 to $3,400 a month (unverified).
Strengths: quick setup (2 to 3 weeks reported), a good mobile approval app, very comfortable for QuickBooks-only companies.
Gaps we have seen: two-way matching only with no configurable three-way tolerance rules; no EU data residency; SOC 2 Type I at last check; no SAP connector.
We tend to win: multi-entity companies, purchase-order-heavy buying, SAP or NetSuite with custom fields, EU data needs.
We tend to lose: small teams with simple non-PO invoices that choose on price.
Guidance: do not disparage. Ask which matching rules the prospect needs, then let them compare.

BOOKWISE AP
Typical quote for 10,000 invoices a month: about $5,800 a month plus a $20,000 implementation (unverified).
Strengths: long ERP list including Workday, very deep audit trail.
Gaps: implementations of 16 to 20 weeks reported, and per-user pricing that gets expensive with many approvers.
We tend to win: prospects who must be live within a quarter, and companies with hundreds of occasional approvers.

APPROVED TALKING POINTS
Price: Growth at 10,000 invoices a month works out to $0.48 per invoice in subscription fees, against a customer-reported median manual cost of $11.40 per invoice. Do not promise savings to a specific prospect before we have seen their volumes.
Security: the SOC 2 Type II report can be shared under NDA. ISO 27001 is in progress and not yet certified. Say exactly that.
NetSuite: custom fields are mapped through a mapping table configured in week 2 of implementation. The Business Central connector is in beta; production use needs Solutions Engineering sign-off.
Migration: vendor master, open purchase orders and historical bills are imported by CSV or API in 5 to 7 business days. We recommend a two-week parallel run and cutover at the start of a month, so the customer does not have to stop processing invoices.
References: up to two, after NDA, same industry when possible. We do not publish customer names.

WHO WE NEED FROM THE CUSTOMER
A finance owner (about 4 hours a week during implementation), an IT contact with ERP admin rights (about 10 hours in total), and the AP lead. Go-live dates are only committed after a technical scoping call.

WHAT WE DO NOT DO
No custom development on Growth. No on-premise hosting. No guaranteed savings figure.

LECTURE-CTX-G1.title: ECON 201 Week 6 notes: money, inflation, Phillips curve
LECTURE-CTX-G1.text:
ECON 201 - Principles of Macroeconomics
Lecture notes, Week 6: Money, Inflation and the Phillips Curve
Lecturer: Prof. Marguerite Halvorsen, Eastbrook University

1. What inflation is
Inflation is a sustained rise in the general price level, measured as the percentage change in a price index. The consumer price index (CPI) compares the cost of a fixed basket of goods today with the cost of the same basket in a base year: CPI = (cost of basket today / cost of basket in base year) x 100. Example: the basket cost 400 dollars in the base year and costs 432 dollars today, so CPI = 108, meaning prices are 8 percent higher than in the base year.

2. Quantity theory of money
The identity is MV = PY, where M is the money supply, V is velocity (how often a unit of money changes hands), P is the price level and Y is real output. If V and Y are roughly stable, growth in M shows up as growth in P. Worked example for the fictional economy of Norvale: M = 500 billion, V = 4, so nominal spending PY = 2,000 billion. Real output Y = 1,000 billion, so P = 2.0. If the central bank raises M by 10 percent to 550 billion while V and Y stay put, PY = 2,200 billion and P = 2.2, a 10 percent rise in prices. Prof. Halvorsen stressed that the "V and Y stable" assumption is the whole argument, and it fails in the short run.

3. Real versus nominal interest rates
Fisher equation: i is approximately r + expected inflation (pi-e), where i is the nominal rate and r is the real rate. Example: a nominal rate of 7 percent with expected inflation of 4 percent gives an expected real rate of about 3 percent. The exact form is (1 + i) = (1 + r)(1 + pi-e). When inflation is unexpected it redistributes wealth: borrowers with fixed-rate loans gain, while lenders and savers holding fixed nominal assets lose.

4. Costs of inflation
Shoe-leather costs (extra trips to the bank to hold less cash), menu costs (the cost of repricing), tax distortions, and uncertainty that makes long-term contracts risky. Extreme case: hyperinflation in Weimar Germany in 1923, when at the peak prices were doubling roughly every four days and workers were paid twice a day so they could spend wages before they lost value.

5. The Phillips curve
The original observation was a short-run inverse relationship between unemployment and inflation. The stagflation of the 1970s (high inflation and high unemployment together) showed that this is not a stable menu that policymakers can choose from. The expectations-augmented version is pi = pi-e - b(u - u*), where u* is the natural rate of unemployment and b measures how strongly inflation responds to the unemployment gap. The curve shifts up when expected inflation rises. In the long run, the curve is vertical at u*, so there is no lasting trade-off.

6. Disinflation case study
Between 1979 and 1982 the US central bank, under Paul Volcker, pushed its policy rate to about 20 percent in 1981. Unemployment rose to about 10.8 percent in 1982, and inflation fell from double digits to roughly 4 percent by 1983. The lost output during a disinflation is often summarized by the "sacrifice ratio".

7. Rule of 72
Years to double is approximately 72 divided by the growth rate in percent. At 3 percent inflation the price level doubles in about 24 years (72 / 3 = 24).

Midterm note: the midterm covers Weeks 1 to 6. Expect one Fisher equation calculation and one short essay on why the Phillips curve shifts. Calculators are allowed. The formula sheet will include only MV = PY.

LECTURE-CTX-G2.title: BIO 110 Lecture 11 notes: cellular respiration
LECTURE-CTX-G2.text:
BIO 110 - Introductory Biology
Lecture 11 notes: Cellular respiration
Lecturer: Dr. Tomasz Reidel, Eastbrook University

Overall reaction
C6H12O6 + 6 O2 -> 6 CO2 + 6 H2O + energy (some captured as ATP, the rest released as heat). This is a redox process: glucose is oxidized (it loses electrons, in practice hydrogen atoms) and oxygen is reduced. Memory aid: OIL RIG, oxidation is loss, reduction is gain.

Stage 1: Glycolysis
Location: cytosol. One glucose (6 carbons) is split into two pyruvate (3 carbons each). Four ATP are made but two are spent to start the process, so the net gain is 2 ATP, plus 2 NADH. No oxygen is needed.

Stage 2: Pyruvate oxidation
Location: mitochondrial matrix. Each pyruvate becomes acetyl-CoA, releasing one CO2 and making one NADH. Per glucose that is 2 CO2 and 2 NADH.

Stage 3: Krebs cycle (citric acid cycle)
Location: mitochondrial matrix. The cycle turns twice per glucose. Per glucose it produces 4 CO2, 6 NADH, 2 FADH2 and 2 ATP.

Stage 4: Oxidative phosphorylation
Location: inner mitochondrial membrane. NADH and FADH2 hand their electrons to the electron transport chain. As electrons move along the chain, protons are pumped into the intermembrane space, building a proton gradient. ATP synthase lets the protons flow back into the matrix and uses that flow to make ATP (chemiosmosis). Oxygen is the final electron acceptor and ends up as water. Without oxygen the chain backs up and the earlier stages stall.

ATP yield
About 2.5 ATP per NADH and about 1.5 ATP per FADH2, giving roughly 30 to 32 ATP per glucose. Older textbooks quote 36 to 38 because they assumed 3 ATP per NADH and 2 per FADH2 and ignored the cost of moving ATP, ADP and NADH across the mitochondrial membranes. Proton leak also lowers the real yield, so the modern figure is lower.

Fermentation
Without oxygen, pyruvate is converted to lactate (animal muscle) or to ethanol and CO2 (yeast). The purpose is to regenerate NAD+ so glycolysis can keep running. The yield is only the 2 ATP from glycolysis.

Poisons and heat
Cyanide blocks the last complex of the electron transport chain, so the chain stops. Brown fat contains an uncoupling protein that lets protons leak back across the membrane, so the energy is released as heat instead of ATP.

Exam note: know the location, inputs and outputs of each stage, and be able to explain why oxygen matters. There is a short quiz on Friday.

LECTURE-CTX-G3.title: HIST 214 Lecture 4 notes: the first Industrial Revolution
LECTURE-CTX-G3.text:
HIST 214 - Modern Britain
Lecture 4 notes: Why Britain? The first Industrial Revolution
Lecturer: Prof. Ifeoma Castellanos, Eastbrook University

Background: the farm economy
The enclosure movement consolidated open fields into private farms. Yields rose and fewer farm workers were needed, so displaced rural labour drifted into towns and later into factories. Prof. Castellanos called enclosure "the front door of the story".

Resources and markets
Britain had abundant coal, navigable rivers and, later, canals. Overseas trade supplied capital, raw cotton and export markets for finished cloth.

Textile mechanization
Flying shuttle, 1733 (John Kay). Spinning jenny, 1764 (James Hargreaves): one worker could spin several threads at once, but it was small and hand-powered, so it suited cottage workshops. Water frame, 1769 (Richard Arkwright): it produced stronger thread but needed water power, so production moved into mills beside rivers, and that is the start of the factory system. Power loom, 1785 (Edmund Cartwright).

Transport
Canals built in the late 1700s made moving coal and raw cotton much cheaper, and railways followed in the 1830s, which tied the growing industrial towns to ports and to each other. Prof. Castellanos noted that cheaper transport also widened the market, so a mill could sell far beyond its own town.

Steam
The Newcomen engine, early 1700s, pumped water out of mines and burned huge amounts of coal. James Watt's separate condenser, patented in 1769, made engines far more efficient. Steam freed factories from riverbanks and let them move to cities near coal and labour.

Social consequences
Manchester grew from a market town into a city of several hundred thousand people by the mid-1800s. Working conditions were harsh, including child labour. The Factory Act of 1833 limited working hours for children in textile mills.

The lecturer's own view
Prof. Castellanos said there is no single cause, and that historians disagree. Some stress institutions and property rights, including the settlement after the Glorious Revolution of 1688, and others stress culture and ideas. If forced to pick, she gives the most weight to energy: cheap, accessible coal is what made steam power pay for itself, and steam is what made the factory city possible. She described institutions and markets as "necessary but not sufficient".

Essay note: the essay is due in Week 7, at 1,500 words, on the question "Was the Industrial Revolution inevitable?" Use at least three primary sources. Reading for this week: chapters 3 and 4 of the course reader.

LECTURE-CTX-C1.title: STAT 101 Week 4 handout: p-values and confidence intervals
LECTURE-CTX-C1.text:
STAT 101 - Week 4 handout: p-values and confidence intervals
Instructor: Dr. Priyanka Vashti, Eastbrook University

Section 1. What a p-value is
A p-value is the probability of seeing data at least as extreme as ours, assuming the null hypothesis is true. It is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true.

Section 2. Worked example: the cafe
A cafe claims its average wait is 70 seconds. We sample n = 25 customers and find a mean wait of 74 seconds with a sample standard deviation s = 10. Standard error = s / sqrt(n) = 10 / 5 = 2 seconds. The test statistic is (74 - 70) / 2 = 2.0.

Section 3. The 95 percent confidence interval
Critical value for 95 percent confidence: z = 1.96. Margin of error = critical value x standard error. Using z = 1.65 for 95 percent confidence, the margin of error is 1.65 x 2 = 3.3 seconds, so the interval is 70.7 to 77.3 seconds. Since our sample mean of 72 seconds sits inside this interval, we cannot distinguish it from the claim.

Section 4. Decision rule
Choose a significance level alpha in advance, usually 0.05. Reject the null hypothesis when the p-value is smaller than alpha. For a larger check, with n = 36 the standard error would shrink to 10 / 6 = 1.67 seconds and the same 4-second gap would be even more convincing.

Quick summary box (read this before the quiz)
- The p-value tells you the chance that the null hypothesis is true.
- If p > 0.05, reject the null hypothesis.
- A 95 percent confidence interval uses z = 1.96.
- Bigger samples give smaller standard errors.

Note: a "large sample" means the sample is big enough for the normal approximation to work. Roughly 30 or more is the usual rule of thumb, but this handout does not say exactly where the line is.
LECTURE-CTX-C1.notes: p-value defined correctly in Section 1 but as "chance null is true" in the summary box; z=1.96 vs z=1.65 both labeled 95 percent; sample mean 74 vs 72 seconds; n=25 vs n=36 for the standard error; decision rule "reject if p < alpha" vs summary "reject if p > 0.05"; "large sample" threshold left undefined.

TECH-CTX-G1.title: Take-home brief: Maintenance Window Consolidator
TECH-CTX-G1.text:
Halden Labs - Backend Engineer Take-Home
Problem: Maintenance Window Consolidator

Background
Halden Labs operates a fleet-management platform. Operations teams schedule maintenance windows for each region, and the scheduling service emits them as flat records. Before windows are shown on the ops calendar, overlapping or touching windows in the same region must be consolidated into one.

Input
A list of records. Each record has:
- region: a string, case-sensitive, at most 32 characters
- start: integer epoch seconds
- end: integer epoch seconds, always greater than start

Output
For every region, the consolidated windows sorted by start time. Two windows in the same region are merged when they overlap or when one ends exactly at the second the other starts. Windows in different regions never merge. The function must not modify its input.

Limits
- Up to 2,000,000 records per run.
- Up to 500 distinct regions.
- The input is not sorted in any way and may contain exact duplicate records.
- Timestamps fit in a signed 64-bit integer.
- The grading machine gives your process 2 vCPUs and 256 MB of memory.
- A full run must finish in 10 seconds.

Examples
Region eu-west with windows (100, 200), (150, 300), (300, 400) consolidates to one window (100, 400), because the last window starts exactly when the merged one ends.
Region us-east with windows (10, 20) and (30, 40) stays as two windows.

Part 2, discussion only
In the follow-up interview we will ask how your design changes if windows arrive as a live stream, possibly out of order by up to five minutes, and the calendar must always show consolidated data. You do not need to implement this part.

Deliverables
1. Your solution in Python, Java, Go or TypeScript.
2. Unit tests, including at least one case with more than one region.
3. A README of at most one page containing the time and space complexity of your solution and any assumptions you made.
4. A short note on how you checked performance at the upper limits.

How we review
Reviewers read for correctness first, then clarity, then performance. Our hidden checks include empty input, a single record, all records in one region, all records identical, and 2,000,000 records spread over 500 regions. A solution that is correct but exceeds the memory limit is marked as failing the performance checks. Please do not use third-party libraries beyond the standard library of your language.

Submission
Send a zip file or a repository link to your recruiter contact, Priya Raman, within 72 hours of receiving this brief. Questions about the problem are welcome and will be answered within one business day.

TECH-CTX-G2.title: Technical interview scorecard
TECH-CTX-G2.text:
Halden Labs - Technical Interview Scorecard
Shared with candidates before the onsite loop so that everyone knows what is being looked at.

Format
The loop has three technical rounds of 45 minutes each: a coding round, a system design round, and a code discussion round based on your take-home. Each round is scored from 1 (strong no) to 4 (strong yes) on the dimensions below. Interviewers write their feedback independently before the debrief.

Coding round
- Clarifying questions: does the candidate confirm inputs, limits and edge cases before writing code?
- Approach before code: is a plan stated, including a simple baseline, before the optimized version?
- Correctness: does the final code work on the examples and on edge cases such as empty input and duplicates?
- Verification: does the candidate trace at least one example by hand and think of their own cases?
- Complexity: can the candidate state and justify time and space cost, including recursion stack and hidden costs?
- Communication: does the candidate think out loud and respond to hints?
Interviewers may give up to two hints. Each hint is noted, and a solution reached with more than one hint cannot score above a 3.

System design round
- Requirements: functional and non-functional requirements agreed within the first ten minutes.
- Estimates: rough numbers for traffic, storage and bandwidth, with the arithmetic shown.
- Interface and data model: the main API calls and the core entities.
- High-level design: components and how a request flows through them.
- Deep dive: the candidate picks one or two areas, such as storage, caching or fan-out, and goes into depth.
- Trade-offs: alternatives named, reasons given, failure modes discussed.
Reaching for a distributed solution when a single database would do is scored down. Not knowing a specific technology is fine if the reasoning is sound.

Code discussion round
We walk through your take-home. Expect questions on complexity, edge cases, and what you would change for streaming input or for ten times the load.

What we do not score
Typing speed, memorized syntax, which of the four supported languages you choose, or whether you use an IDE-style editor or a plain text editor.

What tends to lower a score
- Long silences.
- Announcing an answer without checking it against an example.
- Claiming a complexity without explaining it.
- Ignoring the limits given in the problem statement.
- Adding components that nobody asked for and cannot be justified.

Logistics
Please bring a laptop, or ask us to provide one. Interviewers do not share their scores with each other until the debrief. If a round ends early, the remaining time is not carried over to the next round.

TECH-CTX-G3.title: Candidate's own code file: session_cache.py
TECH-CTX-G3.text:
session_cache.py
Submission for the Kestrel gateway coding exercise. Author: Marta Ilves.

---- File header ----
"""
In-memory session cache for the Kestrel gateway.

Design notes
- get and put are O(1). One dict holds values and another dict holds expiry times.
  A list keeps recency order so I can find the least recently used key.
- Entries expire ttl_seconds after they are written. Expired entries are removed
  lazily, only when someone calls get on them.
- Capacity is bounded. When the cache is full, the least recently used key is evicted.
- I have not tried it with more than one process.

Known limitations
- No locking. The gateway runs one worker thread per connection in dev, and I have
  not added a lock yet.
- No metrics.
"""

---- Code ----
import time


class SessionCache:
    def __init__(self, capacity, ttl_seconds):
        self.capacity = capacity
        self.ttl = ttl_seconds
        self.values = {}
        self.expires = {}
        self.order = []  # least recently used first

    def get(self, key):
        if key not in self.values:
            return None
        if self.expires[key] <= time.time():
            self._drop(key)
            return None
        self.order.remove(key)
        self.order.append(key)
        return self.values[key]

    def put(self, key, value):
        if key in self.values:
            self.values[key] = value
            self.order.remove(key)
            self.order.append(key)
            return
        if len(self.values) >= self.capacity:
            oldest = self.order[0]
            self._drop(oldest)
        self.values[key] = value
        self.expires[key] = time.time() + self.ttl
        self.order.append(key)

    def _drop(self, key):
        self.values.pop(key, None)
        self.expires.pop(key, None)
        if key in self.order:
            self.order.remove(key)

    def size(self):
        return len(self.values)

---- Test notes ----
I wrote three tests with a capacity of 3 and a ttl of 1 second:
1. put then get returns the stored value.
2. Adding a fourth key evicts the key that was read least recently.
3. After sleeping 1.1 seconds, get returns None.
I did not write a test for updating a key that already exists.

---- Decisions ----
I chose a plain list for recency because it was the quickest thing to write in the time limit, and the capacities I tried were small. I considered the standard library's OrderedDict but wanted to show that I understood the mechanics. If the gateway were to hold hundreds of thousands of sessions I would revisit this. I would also add a background sweep so expired entries do not sit in memory forever.

TECH-CTX-G4.title: System design brief: Shortlinks service
TECH-CTX-G4.text:
Orbit Mail - System Design Round Brief
Topic: Shortlinks service

Shared with the candidate 24 hours before the interview. Please read it, but you are not expected to prepare slides. The interviewer will start from this brief and ask follow-up questions.

Product context
Orbit Mail is a fictional email marketing tool. Customers paste long tracking URLs into campaigns, and Orbit turns them into short links such as orb.it/k3Fz9a. Recipients click the short link, are redirected to the original URL, and the customer sees click counts.

Functional requirements
- Create a short link from a long URL through an API call.
- Optional custom alias, up to 30 characters, if it is not already taken.
- Redirect from the short link to the long URL.
- Optional expiry date set by the customer.
- Daily click counts per link, visible in a dashboard within a few minutes of the click.
- Block links that point to domains on the abuse list.

Non-functional requirements
- Redirect latency: p99 under 80 ms.
- Availability: 99.95 percent for redirects. Link creation may be slightly less available.
- Links are kept for five years.
- Traffic comes from the US, the EU and India.

Numbers we use internally
- About 30 million new links per month.
- Reads to writes: roughly 100 to 1.
- Peak traffic is about five times the daily average.
- Average long URL: 200 bytes. Average stored record with metadata: 500 bytes.
- Click events must not be lost, but they may be counted a little late.

Explicitly out of scope
- Link previews.
- QR code generation.
- User accounts and billing.

Open questions the interviewer may raise
- How are short codes generated, and how long should they be?
- What if two customers shorten the same long URL?
- Where do click counts live, and how do they get there?
- What changes if link creation grows ten times?
- How do you keep redirects fast when a link is suddenly very popular?

Notes for the candidate
Numbers above are estimates and can be challenged. You may make your own assumptions as long as you state them. The interviewer cares more about the reasoning behind each choice than about naming a specific database.

TECH-CTX-C1.title: Cluster Count problem statement (draft 3)
TECH-CTX-C1.text:
Cluster Count - Problem Statement (draft 3)

You are given n servers and a list of direct network links between them. Two servers belong to the same cluster if they are connected by any chain of links. Return the number of clusters.

Input
- n, the number of servers. Servers are numbered from 0 to n - 1.
- links, a list of pairs [a, b], each meaning server a has a direct link to server b.

Constraints
- 1 <= n <= 100,000
- 0 <= number of links <= 200,000
- Each pair appears at most once in links.
- Links are undirected.

Requirements
- Your solution must run in O(n + m) time, where m is the number of links.
- Use at most O(n) extra memory.

Notes from the platform team (added later)
- The stress runs use n up to 1,000,000,000 with the links given as an n by n adjacency matrix, so make sure your solution handles that.
- Because the stress runs are large, O(n log n) time is acceptable.
- Servers in the stress runs are numbered from 1 to n.
- In production, a link from a to b is one-way, so a link from a to b does not mean b can reach a. Count clusters the way you think is most useful.
- Duplicate links show up in real data. Ignore them.

Example
n = 5, links = [[0,1],[1,2],[3,4]] returns 2.

Please explain your reasoning in your submission, including any assumptions you had to make about the input.
TECH-CTX-C1.notes: n limit 100,000 vs 1,000,000,000; edge list vs n-by-n matrix; O(n+m) required vs O(n log n) acceptable; 0-indexed vs 1-indexed; undirected vs one-way links; pairs unique vs duplicates present; O(n) memory vs adjacency matrix.

SEMINAR-CTX-G1.title: Slide deck: weekly SMS reminders and household water filter upkeep (public health cluster trial)
SEMINAR-CTX-G1.text:
SLIDE 1. Title
Weekly Text Reminders and Household Water Filter Upkeep: A Cluster-Randomised Trial in Harrowmere District
Dr. Ilse Brandvold, Harrowmere Institute of Community Health
Departmental seminar, 14 March 2025
Trial registry ID: HCT-2024-0117

SLIDE 2. Background
- Ceramic household water filters were handed out to 6,400 households in Harrowmere District in 2022.
- A 2023 survey found that 38% of filters had a cracked or bypassed element by 12 months.
- Diarrhoeal illness in children under 5 is still the district's leading reason for clinic visits in that age group.
- Question: can cheap reminders keep filters working after the handout?

SLIDE 3. Hypotheses (pre-registered)
- H1: Weekly SMS reminders lower 7-day diarrhoea prevalence in children under 5.
- H2: Reminders raise the share of households with a functioning filter at follow-up.
- H1 is the primary outcome. Everything else is secondary.

SLIDE 4. Design
- Cluster-randomised: 60 villages, 30 per arm.
- 1,812 households enrolled between June and August 2024 (about 30 per village).
- Randomisation at village level, stratified by distance to the nearest clinic (5 km or less, or more than 5 km).
- Sample size: assumed intracluster correlation of 0.05; 80% power to detect a fall in prevalence from 16% (pilot estimate) to 10%.
- Follow-up survey at 26 weeks; the last surveys finished in February 2025.
- Enumerators for the diarrhoea survey did not know each village's arm. Households could not be blinded.

SLIDE 5. Intervention and control
- Reminder arm: one SMS every Tuesday at 17:00 for 26 weeks, in the local language, Karvi.
- Each message said three things: clean the ceramic element, look for cracks, keep filtered water in a covered container.
- Control arm: the original handout only, no messages.
- Cost: USD 0.011 per SMS, so about USD 0.29 per household over 26 weeks. One-off platform set-up: USD 1,150.

SLIDE 6. Measures and analysis
- Primary: caregiver-reported diarrhoea in the past 7 days in children under 5 (three or more loose stools in 24 hours).
- Secondary: functioning filter, defined as an observed flow of at least 1.0 litre per hour; filtered-water turbidity below 5 NTU.
- Follow-up completed in 1,764 of 1,812 households (48 lost, 2.6%).
- Children under 5 measured: 902 in reminder villages, 874 in control villages.
- Analysis: intention to treat, generalised estimating equations with village as the cluster.

SLIDE 7. Results
Outcome | Reminder | Control | Estimate (95% CI)
7-day diarrhoea, children under 5 | 11.4% | 15.8% | risk ratio 0.72 (0.55 to 0.95)
Functioning filter (flow at least 1.0 L/h) | 64.2% | 47.9% | difference 16.3 points (9.8 to 22.7)
Filtered water below 5 NTU | 81.0% | 70.3% | difference 10.7 points (3.4 to 18.0)
All estimates account for clustering by village.

SLIDE 8. Subgroups (exploratory)
- Villages more than 5 km from a clinic: risk ratio 0.61 (0.42 to 0.89).
- Villages 5 km or less from a clinic: risk ratio 0.83 (0.58 to 1.19).
- Interaction: p = 0.21. This was not a pre-registered confirmatory comparison.

SLIDE 9. Delivery
- The SMS gateway logged 91% of messages as delivered.
- We could not verify that messages were read.
- Control households were not contacted about their filters during the trial.

SLIDE 10. Limitations
- Diarrhoea is caregiver-reported, so it may be affected by recall and social desirability. No stool samples were collected.
- One follow-up window only: 26 weeks.
- Contamination between neighbouring villages was not checked.
- Every household had the same ceramic filter model, so results may not carry over to other filters.
- No cost-effectiveness analysis was done in this trial.

SLIDE 11. Conclusions and next steps
- Weekly SMS reminders were associated with a 28% lower relative risk of diarrhoea and better filter function at 26 weeks.
- Next trial (planned for 2026): weekly versus fortnightly messages.
- Not yet studied: durability beyond 26 weeks, other filter types, cost per case averted.

SLIDE 12. Funding
Harrowmere Regional Health Fund, grant RHF-22-408. The funder had no role in the analysis.

SEMINAR-CTX-G2.title: Paper excerpt: TidalLog compaction scheduling for embedded key-value stores (computer systems)
SEMINAR-CTX-G2.text:
TidalLog: Load-Aware Compaction Scheduling for Embedded Key-Value Stores on Flash Storage
Marek Oyelaran and Thi Han Vuong, Corvane Polytechnic
Workshop on Storage for Small Devices, 2025

ABSTRACT
Embedded key-value stores built on log-structured merge (LSM) trees suffer from write amplification and unpredictable read tail latency when compaction runs on fixed thresholds regardless of foreground load. We present TidalLog, a compaction scheduler that estimates a "tide" signal, the ratio of the recent foreground write rate to the device's smoothed sustainable write rate, and defers or advances compaction accordingly. On a quad-core ARM board with eMMC storage, TidalLog cuts write amplification by 34% on a write-heavy workload and p99 read latency by 21% on a balanced workload relative to a fixed-threshold baseline, at a cost of 4.1 MB of extra memory.

1. RELATED WORK
Fixed-ratio leveled compaction, which we call StaticLevel (size ratio 10), is the default in many embedded stores. LazyTier uses tiered compaction to lower write amplification but leaves more overlapping files, which raises read cost. BurstGuard rate-limits compaction when the foreground request queue grows past a length threshold; it does not consider device capacity and was evaluated only on read-heavy traces. Workload-predictive schedulers exist for server-class SSDs. We do not evaluate them because they need more memory than our target devices have.

2. METHOD
Every 5-second window, TidalLog computes w, the bytes written by the foreground in that window, and divides by S, an exponentially weighted moving average (alpha = 0.2) of the device throughput measured during compaction bursts. The smoothed ratio is the tide T. When T is above 0.7 (high tide), compaction of level 2 and deeper is deferred, for at most 3 consecutive windows (15 seconds). When T is below 0.3 (low tide), compaction is advanced: the level with the highest overlap score is compacted opportunistically. Level 0 is exempt: it compacts once it holds 8 files, and writes stall at 12 files. The implementation is about 2,900 lines of C++17 on top of MicroLSM, our in-house open-source store. The thresholds 0.7 and 0.3 were chosen by grid search (0.5 to 0.9 and 0.1 to 0.4) on workload W-B only.

3. EXPERIMENTAL SETUP
Hardware: quad-core ARM Cortex-A53 at 1.4 GHz, 2 GB RAM, 32 GB eMMC 5.1. Workloads: W-A write-heavy (80% writes), W-B balanced (50% writes), W-C read-heavy (5% writes). Each workload issues 64 million operations with 16-byte keys and 240-byte values under a Zipfian key distribution (theta = 0.9). Each configuration was run 5 times and we report means. We compare StaticLevel, LazyTier, BurstGuard and TidalLog.

4. RESULTS
Table 1. Main results (means of 5 runs)
System | Write amplification (W-A) | p99 read latency, ms (W-B) | Throughput, kops/s (W-A)
StaticLevel | 14.2 | 9.8 | 18.4
LazyTier | 9.7 | 14.6 | 21.9
BurstGuard | 12.5 | 8.9 | 19.1
TidalLog | 9.4 | 7.7 | 22.6

Run-to-run standard deviation was at most 0.4 for write amplification and 0.6 ms for p99 latency. On W-C, p99 read latency was within 3% across all four systems. Over the W-A run, StaticLevel performed 1.92 million block erases and TidalLog 1.27 million. Sensitivity to the smoothing factor: alpha = 0.1 gave write amplification 9.9, alpha = 0.2 gave 9.4, alpha = 0.4 gave 9.6. Crash consistency: we injected 200 power losses during W-B; every run recovered with no acknowledged write lost.

5. LIMITATIONS
We used one board and one storage type (eMMC); we did not evaluate NVMe or SD cards. Workloads are synthetic with fixed value sizes. The tide thresholds were tuned on W-B and not re-tuned per workload. Five runs per configuration is a small sample and we report no formal significance tests. We did not study multi-tenant setups or wear beyond 64 million operations. Deferral of up to 15 seconds can let compaction debt build up under sustained bursts.

6. CONCLUSION
TidalLog is a low-overhead scheduler that lowers write amplification and tail latency on flash-backed embedded stores without changing the on-disk format. Future work includes per-level thresholds and multi-device setups.

SEMINAR-CTX-G3.title: Thesis chapter: pollinator visitation in restored grassland fragments (ecology)
SEMINAR-CTX-G3.text:
CHAPTER 4. POLLINATOR VISITATION IN RESTORED CALCAREOUS GRASSLAND FRAGMENTS
Sofia Ekwueme-Lindqvist, PhD thesis, University of Northhaven, 2025

4.1 RESEARCH QUESTIONS
RQ1: Does fragment area predict pollinator species richness?
RQ2: Does distance to the nearest source grassland predict visitation rate?
RQ3: Does time since restoration predict visitation rate once area and distance are accounted for?
We expected richness to rise with area and visitation to fall with distance. For restoration age we had no prior expectation, so RQ3 is exploratory.

4.2 METHODS
Study system. We surveyed 24 restored fragments in the Vellmark Hills. Fragment area ranged from 0.4 to 11.2 ha, and fragments had been restored between 3 and 19 years before the study. Source grasslands were remnant, never-ploughed sites larger than 40 ha.
Sampling. Each fragment was surveyed four times per season (May, June, July, August) in 2022 and 2023, between 10:00 and 16:00, in dry conditions above 14 degrees C. At each visit, observers ran eight timed 10-minute watches at 1 square metre patches of flowering plants. Three observers collected the data. Bees were netted under permit and identified to species from voucher specimens. Hoverflies and butterflies were identified from photographs and field keys; 9% of hoverfly visits could only be assigned to genus. Moths were not sampled.
Analysis. Species richness was modelled with a Poisson generalised linear mixed model (GLMM) and visitation rate (visits per hour of watch) with a negative binomial GLMM. Both had fragment as a random intercept and year as a fixed effect. Predictors were log10 area, distance to the nearest source grassland (m), restoration age (years) and floral cover (percentage points). Spatial autocorrelation in residuals was checked with Moran's I.

4.3 RESULTS
We recorded 14,207 visits by 71 species: 38 bees, 21 hoverflies and 12 butterflies. The Chao2 estimator put true richness at 83 species (SE 6). The smallest fragments (under 1 ha, n = 5) held 9 to 17 species; the largest (over 8 ha, n = 4) held 31 to 44.

Table 4.1. GLMM results
Response | Predictor | Estimate | 95% CI | p
Species richness | log10 area | rate ratio 1.36 per tenfold increase | 1.12 to 1.65 | 0.002
Visitation rate | distance to source | rate ratio 0.92 per 100 m | 0.87 to 0.97 | 0.003
Visitation rate | restoration age | rate ratio 1.01 per year | 0.98 to 1.04 | 0.48
Visitation rate | floral cover | rate ratio 1.06 per percentage point | 1.04 to 1.08 | <0.001
Moran's I on residuals: p = 0.41. Area and floral cover were moderately correlated (r = 0.44).

4.4 DISCUSSION
RQ1 was supported, in line with a species-area relationship. RQ2 was supported: at 0.92 per 100 m, a fragment 500 m from a source grassland is expected to receive roughly a third fewer visits than one adjacent to it. This fits the limited foraging ranges reported in the literature for small solitary bees, although we did not measure foraging range here. For RQ3 we found no evidence of an effect of restoration age. This may reflect variation in seed mix and management between sites, which we did not quantify. Floral cover was the strongest single predictor of visitation.

4.5 THREATS TO VALIDITY
- Only two seasons were sampled. 2022 was a drought summer (July rainfall was 38% of the 30-year mean) and floral cover was lower that year.
- Fragments were chosen by landowner access, not at random.
- Three observers took part. Calibration walks reduced but did not remove differences between them, and observer identity was not included in the models.
- Visits are not pollination: no pollen-load data were collected.
- Nocturnal pollinators were not sampled.
- Land use in the surrounding matrix was not controlled.
- All results are correlational.

SEMINAR-CTX-G4.title: Experiment writeup: RetrievalPath spaced retrieval practice with ablation (education)
SEMINAR-CTX-G4.text:
RetrievalPath: Adaptive Spaced Retrieval Practice in a First-Year Statistics Course
Annika Feldmarsh and Tobias Quenby, Westerlund College. Technical report WC-EDU-TR-12, January 2025

1. SYSTEM
RetrievalPath is a plugin for the course learning platform that serves short retrieval quizzes. The item bank holds 640 multiple-choice and short-numeric items tagged to 11 topics. It has three components. (a) Difficulty estimator: each item carries an Elo-style rating updated after every response (K = 24), and items are chosen to target a 75% success rate for the student. (b) Interval scheduler: after a correct answer the next review interval is multiplied by 2.2 if the student reported high confidence and by 1.4 if low confidence; after an incorrect answer the interval resets to 1 day. (c) Confidence prompt: before seeing feedback, the student rates confidence on a 3-point scale.

2. STUDY DESIGN
The study ran in the autumn 2024 semester (12 teaching weeks) across six sections of STAT 101. 449 students enrolled and consented, and were randomised individually within section to four conditions:
- Control: a standard weekly 10-item quiz, no adaptation.
- Full: all three components.
- No adaptation: difficulty-matched selection and expanding intervals replaced by a fixed 3-day repeat of randomly chosen items.
- No confidence prompts: the prompt removed and a single multiplier of 1.8 used after every correct answer.
The analysis sample is the 412 students who sat the final exam (37, or 8.2%, did not). Ethics approval: WC-EDU-2024-31. The primary outcome is the final exam score (0 to 100), marked by instructors from anonymised scripts. The secondary outcome is an unannounced delayed retention quiz (0 to 40) given 4 weeks after the end of term; 331 of the 412 students (80.3%) took it.

3. RESULTS
Table 1. Outcomes by condition
Condition | n | Final exam, mean (SD) | Delayed retention, mean (of 40)
Control weekly quiz | 103 | 68.1 (14.2) | 19.8
Full RetrievalPath | 105 | 74.9 (13.6) | 26.3
No adaptation | 102 | 71.0 (14.0) | 22.9
No confidence prompts | 102 | 73.6 (13.9) | 25.4

Full versus Control on the final exam: +6.8 points, Cohen's d = 0.49 (95% CI 0.21 to 0.77), p = 0.001. On delayed retention the difference was +6.5 points out of 40. Ablation: removing adaptation gave up 3.9 points, 57% of the total gain (Holm-adjusted p = 0.048 for Full versus No adaptation). Removing confidence prompts gave up 1.3 points, 19% of the gain (adjusted p = 0.41). Usage: students in the Full condition completed a median of 24 sessions and 71% completed at least 20; the median for No adaptation and No confidence prompts was 23 and 24 sessions. Median session length was 9 minutes.

4. DEPLOYMENT
Median time to serve an item was 180 ms (95th percentile 640 ms). Server cost for the semester was about USD 310. Instructors spent 14 hours tagging the item bank to topics.

5. LIMITATIONS
One course, one college, one semester. Students were not blind to condition. Sharing of tips between students within a section may have leaked some effects across conditions. Only 80.3% of students took the delayed quiz, so selective drop-out is possible, and retention results are for those who took it. The analysis plan was written before the exam but was not publicly registered. A planned subgroup analysis for first-generation students is not reported because the subgroups are too small. Difficulty matching and expanding intervals were removed together in the No adaptation condition, so the ablation cannot separate their contributions.

6. CONCLUSION
Adaptive scheduling accounts for most of the measured benefit. The confidence prompt made a smaller contribution whose statistical support is weak. We plan a pre-registered replication across two courses in 2025-26.

SEMINAR-CTX-I1.title: Slide deck: tone sandhi in Ostrelle compound nouns (linguistics)
SEMINAR-CTX-I1.text:
SLIDE 1. Tone Sandhi in Ostrelle Compound Nouns
Dr. Prakash Venkatesan-Holm, Department of Linguistics, Lower Ridgeway University
Reading group talk, 5 November 2024

SLIDE 2. The phenomenon
- Ostrelle is a small tonal language variety with three lexical tones: high (H), mid (M) and low (L).
- In two-noun compounds the tone of the first noun changes when the second noun begins with a high tone.
- Earlier descriptions treated this as a fixed rule. We ask whether it depends on how frequent the compound is.

SLIDE 3. Data
- Elicited recordings from native speakers in the river villages, 2023.
- 214 compound nouns, each read three times in a carrier sentence.
- Pitch measured at five points along the first syllable.

SLIDE 4. Findings
- L + H compounds: the first tone rises to M in 83% of tokens.
- M + H compounds: the first tone rises to H in 61% of tokens.
- H + H compounds: no change in 97% of tokens.
- More frequent compounds showed the change more often, but the effect was small.

SLIDE 5. Analysis note
- Frequency comes from a written corpus of local radio scripts, 1.4 million words.
- Change rates are reported per compound type, not per speaker.

SLIDE 6. Open questions
- Does the pattern hold in spontaneous speech?
- Do younger speakers apply the rule less often?
- How should we treat borrowed compounds?

SEMINAR-CTX-C1.title: Slide deck: flywheel assist for municipal bus depots (transport engineering)
SEMINAR-CTX-C1.text:
SLIDE 1. Flywheel Assist for Municipal Bus Depots: Trial Results
Lorcan Adeyemi-Fisk, Tarnbrook Transit Authority
Depot managers briefing, October 2024

SLIDE 2. Context
- Tarnbrook Transit runs 120 diesel buses from two depots, Millgate and Eastfield.
- We ran a 6-month trial (February to July 2024) of a flywheel regenerative-braking assist on Route family 14.
- 48 buses at Millgate depot were fitted.

SLIDE 3. Method
- Baseline period: November 2023 to January 2024, before fitting.
- Fuel logged per shift by on-board telematics, compared with the same buses' baseline.
- Buses with telematics faults were excluded from the analysis.

SLIDE 4. Headline
- Fuel use down 31% on fitted buses.
- Brake pad replacements per bus per year fell from 3.1 to 2.4.

SLIDE 5. Results table
Metric | Baseline | Trial
Buses in analysis | 42 | 42
Fuel use, L per 100 km | 41.2 | 32.6
Change in fuel use | - | -20.9%
Trial dates | - | 1 February to 30 September 2024
p-value (paired by bus) | - | 0.09
Brake pad replacements per bus per year | 3.1 | 2.4

SLIDE 6. Cost
- Capital cost of fitting the buses, installation included: USD 1.86 million.
- Annual fuel and maintenance saving: USD 0.31 million.
- Payback: under 3 years.

SLIDE 7. Conclusion
- The retrofit cut fuel use by roughly a quarter, with statistically significant results, and pays back within three years.
- Recommendation: roll out to all 120 buses.

SLIDE 8. Caveats
- One depot only.
- The baseline covers winter months only.
SEMINAR-CTX-C1.notes: Deliberate contradictions: (1) fleet trial length is 6 months (Feb-Jul 2024) on slide 2 but slide 5 gives 1 Feb to 30 Sep 2024 (8 months); (2) 48 buses fitted on slide 2 vs 42 buses in analysis on slide 5, with the exclusion count never stated; (3) fuel saving is 31% on slide 4, -20.9% in the slide 5 table, and "roughly a quarter" in the conclusion; (4) conclusion says statistically significant but the table gives p = 0.09; (5) payback "under 3 years" on slide 6 but USD 1.86M capital / USD 0.31M annual saving implies about 6 years.

CALLCENTER-CTX-G1.title: Halden Home support knowledge base excerpt
CALLCENTER-CTX-G1.text:
HALDEN HOME SUPPORT KNOWLEDGE BASE - AGENT REFERENCE
Revision 3.2, effective 1 September 2026. Halden Home sells fiber internet, mobile plans, and the Halden Box subscription.

1. VERIFICATION
Standard verification is required before discussing any account detail. Collect all of the following: the full name on the account, the 6-digit account PIN, and either the last 4 digits of the payment card or the billing ZIP code. If the customer cannot recall the PIN, the agent may send a one-time code, valid for 10 minutes, to the mobile number or email registered on the account. Agents must never read out, hint at, or confirm a PIN. Agents must never ask a customer to read out a password and must never ask for a full card number.
Changes to email, phone number, password, or shipping address need enhanced verification: the customer must read back the one-time code sent to the contact on file. If the customer has lost access to the registered email, the code goes to the registered mobile number. If neither is available, the customer submits the Identity Review form (photo ID plus a bill from the last 60 days), which is reviewed within 3 business days.
Agents never disclose details of any account other than the verified one, even to a spouse or relative, unless that person is a listed Authorized User.

2. REFUNDS AND RETURNS
Halden Box charges: refundable within 14 days of the charge date if the box has not shipped. Once shipped, the refund is issued after the items are returned.
Devices: 30-day return window from the delivery date. Opened devices carry a 10 percent restocking fee. Defective devices carry no fee.
Duplicate charges: refunded in full with no fee when reported within 90 days of the charge. The refund posts to the original payment method within 5 business days; the customer's bank may take 2 to 3 further business days.
Any refund over $75 needs Tier 2 approval before it is submitted.

3. CANCELLATION
Month-to-month plans can be cancelled at any time. The cancellation takes effect at the end of the current billing period with no fee. There are no partial-month refunds except for duplicate charges.
Retention: one offer per customer every 12 months, 2 months at 30 percent off. Offer it once, and only after the customer says they want to cancel.

4. SHIPPING
Standard delivery is 3 to 5 business days after dispatch. If an order has not arrived 7 business days after dispatch, offer a free reship or a refund.
Package marked delivered but missing: ask the customer to check with neighbors and the building office for 24 hours, then open a carrier trace, which takes 3 business days. After the trace, reship or refund.
Wrong item: send a prepaid return label and ship the replacement within 2 business days. Items valued under $20 do not need to be returned.

5. CONNECTIVITY TROUBLESHOOTING
Router light: solid white means online, blinking amber means no line detected, solid red means a hardware fault.
Steps: (1) power cycle for 30 seconds and wait 2 minutes; (2) check cables and test with a wired connection; (3) run the remote line test, about 90 seconds. If the line test fails, book a technician visit within 3 to 5 days. The visit is free when the fault is on the Halden side and $49 when the fault is in the customer's own wiring or equipment.
Configuration of third-party routers, VLANs, and port forwarding is not supported. Agents may share the public setup guide only.

6. OUTAGE STATUS (as of 09:15 today)
Incident INC-4471: fiber outage in the Ridgemont zone, ZIP codes 30411 and 30412. Started 08:40. Estimated restoration 15:30. Estimates are not guarantees and agents must never promise a time. The automatic outage credit of $1.50 per day applies only when an outage lasts longer than 24 hours.

7. ESCALATION LADDER AND CREDIT AUTHORITY
Tier 1 agent: goodwill credit up to $25.
Tier 2 specialist: credits up to $75, billing exceptions, and any customer contacting for the third time about the same issue.
Team lead: credits up to $250. Handles customers who ask for a manager, after the agent has attempted resolution. Callback within 4 business hours.
Duty manager: legal threats, regulatory complaints, suspected account takeover, and credits above $250.
For suspected account takeover, lock the account first, then notify the duty manager.

8. PRIVACY REQUESTS
Data export and deletion requests are handled only through the Privacy Portal. Agents cannot perform them by phone and cannot confirm what data is held. Response takes up to 30 days.

9. CLOSING A CALL
Recap the resolution and next steps, give the reference number, and note that a follow-up email arrives within 1 hour.

HALDEN HOME KNOWLEDGE BASE - REFUNDS AND ESCALATIONS
Page status: migrated from the old wiki. Sections marked (v2) were written in 2025 and sections marked (v3) in 2026. Both versions are currently visible to agents.

Saturday (E); manager requests transfer immediately (C) vs two documented attempts first (F); Tier 1 credit $25 vs $40 by tenure (G); restocking fee 10 vs 15 percent and 'as applicable' waiver (H); cancellation immediate (I v2) vs end of period (I v3); duty manager regulatory complaints 'at discretion' (J).

FCC-CTX-G1.title: Veltro Mobile agent handbook section 4: account security and SIM services
FCC-CTX-G1.text:
Veltro Mobile Agent Handbook, Section 4: Account Security and SIM Services (revision 12, internal)

4.1 Verification levels
Standard verification: the 6-digit account PIN, OR the account holder's date of birth plus the billing ZIP code. Standard verification is enough to discuss plan details, balances and usage, and to suspend a line reported lost or stolen.
High-risk verification is required for SIM swaps (physical SIM replacement), eSIM transfers to a new device, generating a Number Transfer PIN, changing the account email or billing address, and adding a line. High-risk verification means the account PIN AND a one-time passcode (OTP) texted to a different line on the account, or to the account holder's registered backup number. If the caller cannot receive an OTP on another line (for example, the customer has a single line and that phone is lost or broken), the agent must direct them to a Veltro store with photo ID. There is no agent override for high-risk verification, including for supervisors.

4.2 Fraud Hold
Three failed PIN attempts within 24 hours place the account on Fraud Hold automatically. A Fraud Hold lasts 72 hours. During a Fraud Hold no high-risk action can be completed by phone or in store. Only the Fraud Team can lift a hold early; agents open a case type FRH and the Fraud Team contacts the account holder. Agents cannot lift a hold.

4.3 Unauthorised SIM swap or port-out
If a customer suddenly loses service and suspects a SIM swap or a number port they did not request: (1) complete Standard verification, (2) suspend any active SIM that is not in the customer's hands, (3) open a case type SSW and warm-transfer to the Fraud Team, which is available 24/7. Do not read out or discuss account notes about who made the change, which store or channel was used, or the other device. Advise the customer to contact their bank directly about any activity they did not make. Veltro does not reimburse losses at banks or other third parties; do not promise compensation.

4.4 Lost or stolen devices
Suspending a line stops calls, texts and data but does not pause billing. To blocklist the device itself the customer must provide the IMEI (from the box, the original receipt or the device page in the account). Without the IMEI the device can still be used with another carrier's SIM. Replacement SIM cards ship in 2 business days, free for postpaid accounts and $10 for prepaid accounts. An eSIM can be reissued in store at no charge after high-risk verification. Device insurance claims (VeltroCare) are filed online by the customer, not by agents.

4.5 Number Transfer PIN (leaving Veltro)
Customers moving their number to another carrier need a Number Transfer PIN. It can be generated in the Veltro app or by an agent after high-risk verification, and it is valid for 5 days. Port-outs are blocked while the account is on Fraud Hold. The final bill includes any remaining device installments; agents cannot waive device balances.

4.6 Account PIN resets
Customers can reset the account PIN in the Veltro app using the phone's biometric login, or in store with photo ID. Agents can send a reset link to the account email on file only. Agents must never set a PIN for the customer or read a PIN back.

4.7 Things agents do not do
Agents do not give out other customers' details, confirm whether a number belongs to a Veltro customer, provide call or text logs over the phone (those requests go to legal.requests@veltro.example), or promise timelines owned by other teams.

FCC-CTX-G2.title: Veltro Mobile billing reference: roaming and adjustments
FCC-CTX-G2.text:
Veltro Mobile Billing Reference: International Roaming and Adjustments (revision 9)

R1. TravelPass
TravelPass costs $8 per day and lets postpaid customers use their domestic plan in Zone 1 destinations (138 countries; agents look up individual countries in the destination tool). The daily charge applies only on days the line makes a call, sends a text or uses data while connected to a Zone 1 network. Background data counts as use, so a phone left on with apps refreshing can trigger the daily charge. TravelPass charges are capped at 10 per bill cycle, so a customer never pays more than $80 in TravelPass charges in one cycle. TravelPass must be on the line before the usage happens; it is not applied retroactively.

R2. Zone 2 (not covered by TravelPass)
Cruise ships, ferries with onboard networks and in-flight networks are maritime and aviation networks. They are billed at Zone 2 rates even when TravelPass is active: data $2.05 per MB, calls $3.49 per minute, outgoing texts $0.50 each. Customers can avoid these charges by switching on "Block Zone 2" in the app before they travel.

R3. Roaming dispute adjustments
If a customer disputes roaming charges and TravelPass was active on the line at the time, the agent may credit up to $150 per bill cycle without approval, using reason code RMA. Disputes above $150 go to Billing Review as case type BRV. Billing Review decides within 10 business days and notifies the customer by text. Agents must not promise the outcome of a Billing Review.

R4. Courtesy adjustment for customers without TravelPass
If the customer had no TravelPass, the agent may offer a one-time courtesy adjustment of 50% of the disputed roaming charges, up to $200, once per 24 months per account. Check the "Courtesy used" flag on the account first. If the flag is set, no courtesy adjustment is available by phone.

R5. How adjustments appear
All adjustments appear as a credit on the next bill. Postpaid customers do not receive card refunds for adjustments. Prepaid customers receive adjustments as account balance.

R6. Late fees and autopay
The late fee is $7. Agents may waive one late fee per account per 12 months. The autopay discount is $5 per line per month and applies only when autopay uses a debit card or bank account; since 1 June, autopay by credit card no longer earns the discount.

R7. Network problems
Credits for network problems, such as a local tower outage, are handled by the Network Credits team (case type NWC). Agents cannot set up recurring monthly credits of any kind.

FCC-CTX-C1.title: Veltro roaming FAQ for store staff (handout)
FCC-CTX-C1.text:
Veltro Roaming FAQ for Store Staff (printed handout)

How much is TravelPass?
TravelPass is $10 a day in covered countries. The customer is only charged on days they use the phone abroad.

Is there a cap?
No cap. The customer pays for every day they use it, however long the trip is.

Does TravelPass work on cruise ships?
Yes. TravelPass works on most cruise lines once the ship leaves port, so customers do not need to buy the cruise line's own package.

Can TravelPass be added after the trip?
Yes. If the customer adds TravelPass within 3 days of returning, the call center can re-rate the trip at the TravelPass price.

A customer without TravelPass got a big roaming bill. What can we do?
Store staff cannot adjust bills. Send the customer to the call center, which can credit 100% of the roaming charges once every 12 months as a courtesy.

Quick tips for the counter
- Remind customers that TravelPass tops out at $80 a cycle, so a long trip is never more than that.
- Maritime and in-flight networks are excluded from all roaming packages, including TravelPass. Tell cruise passengers to switch on Block Zone 2.
- Courtesy adjustments are half of the roaming charges, and the account can only get one every two years.
- TravelPass has to be on the line before the customer uses the phone abroad. It never applies backwards.
- The daily price is $8 in every covered country.
- For anything not on this sheet, ask the store manager to call the agent support line before promising the customer anything.
FCC-CTX-C1.notes: Contradicts itself: TravelPass $10 a day vs $8 a day; no cap vs tops out at $80 a cycle; works on cruise ships vs maritime networks excluded from all packages; can be added within 3 days after the trip and re-rated vs never applies backwards; courtesy credit 100% once every 12 months vs half, once every two years.

Harbor Point Condominium Association - Board Meeting Minutes
Date: Thursday, September 24
Location: Community room, Building B
Present: Linda Marsh (President), Owen Castellano (Treasurer), Priya Nair (Secretary), Hal Jensen, Beatriz Soto. Also present: Renee Okoro (property manager, Seaside Management) and 11 owners.
Quorum confirmed. Meeting called to order at 7:02 pm.

1. Approval of August minutes
Approved unanimously without changes.

2. Treasurer's report
Owen Castellano reported the operating account is on budget for the year. The reserve fund balance is $179,500. Delinquent dues stand at three units, total $4,210; the management company has sent second notices.

3. Building A elevator
The Building A elevator has been out of service intermittently since July because of a failing controller. Two quotes were received. The board voted 4-1 (Jensen opposed) to accept the Carver Lift Services quote of $38,500 to replace the controller, paid from the reserve fund. - Summit Exteriors: $236,500

The board voted unanimously to move forward with Kessler Roofing, subject to reference checks and a signed contract. A start date will be negotiated after the contract is signed. Owners raised noise from the pool pump at night (management to check timer), a request for a second bike rack by Building B (board to get a price), and a question about EV charging (no action; to be revisited in spring).

- Renee Okoro: sign Carver contract; order guest hang-tags and distribute by October 10; post elevator updates.

- Priya Nair: circulate new pet registration form to all owners by October 1.

Adjourned 8:41 pm.

FGENH-CTX-G2.title: Charity 10K volunteer briefing
FGENH-CTX-G2.text:
Riverside 10K - Volunteer Briefing

Thank you for volunteering! Race day is Sunday 25 October. About 1,100 runners are registered. Please read this whole sheet; it answers most of what people ask on the morning.

Check-in
All volunteers check in at the volunteer tent next to the finish arch in Alder Park. Course volunteers (water stations and marshals) check in by 6:15 am so we can drive you out before the roads close at 7:15 am. Finish-line and bag-drop volunteers check in by 7:00 am. You will get a volunteer shirt, a lanyard and your station card at check-in. Please wear closed-toe shoes.

Race timing
The race starts at 8:00 am. The lead runners reach the 3K station around 8:10 and the 6K station around 8:19. The course closes at 9:45 am, and the sweep bike passes each station after the last runner; do not pack down until the sweep bike has passed.

Water stations
There are two water stations. The 3K station is on Mill Lane beside the boathouse; station captain is Grace Adeyemi. The 6K station is at the corner of River Road and Hatch Street; station captain is Marcus Bell. Each station has 8 volunteers. Pour cups about two-thirds full, set out the first 200 cups before 8:00, and hold cups out at arm's length with your arm still, not moving toward the runner. Empty cups go in the green bins; there is a litter pick along 100 meters after each station once the course closes.

Marshals
Marshals stand at each turn with a flag. Your job is to point the way and keep spectators off the course. You are not police and cannot stop traffic; if a car tries to enter the course, radio the course director.

Radios and problems
Each station captain carries a radio. Channel 1 is the course director, Sam Ruiz. Channel 2 is the medical lead. If a runner collapses or looks unwell, tell your captain immediately; the captain radios channel 2 and a medical cyclist is sent. Do not move a runner who has fallen unless they are in danger where they are. Lost children go to the volunteer tent.

Weather
We run in rain. If there is lightning, the course director will make the call and captains will be told on channel 1.

After the race
Volunteers are welcome at the finish area for food from 10:00 am. Please return lanyards and radios to the volunteer tent. Shirts are yours to keep.

Volunteer coordinator: Tessa Morgan, volunteers@riverside10k.org.

FGEN-CTX-G2.title: Riverbend Family Clinic - preparing for your annual physical
FGEN-CTX-G2.text:
RIVERBEND FAMILY CLINIC
Preparing for Your Annual Physical

Thank you for booking your annual physical with Riverbend Family Clinic. This sheet explains how to prepare so your visit runs smoothly. Your visit will be with Dr. Hollis Varga or a member of her care team.

Before your visit
- If your provider ordered fasting bloodwork (such as a lipid panel or fasting glucose), do not eat or drink anything except water for 10 hours before your appointment. Please avoid coffee, including black coffee, and chewing gum during the fasting period. Take your usual medications with water unless your provider has told you otherwise.
- Complete the health history questionnaire in the patient portal at least 2 days before your visit. If you cannot use the portal, arrive 30 minutes early to fill it in on paper.
- Make a list of every medication, vitamin and supplement you take, including the dose.

What to bring
- Photo ID and your current insurance card.
- Your medication list.
- Glasses or hearing aids if you use them.
- Any home blood pressure readings from the last month.

Arriving
Please arrive 15 minutes before your appointment time to check in. If you are more than 15 minutes late, we may need to reschedule you. Parking is available in Lot B behind the building; bring your ticket to the front desk for 2 hours of free validated parking. Street parking on Weller Avenue is metered.

During your visit
Your visit includes a review of your history, vital signs, a physical exam, and any screenings recommended for your age. Flu shots are available at no extra charge during your physical from October through March while supplies last. If you have a specific concern, mention it at check-in so enough time can be set aside; a separate appointment may be needed for complex issues.

After your visit
Lab results are posted to the patient portal, usually within 3 business days. Your provider will message you if anything needs follow-up. Normal results may be posted without a personal note. Follow-up visits can often be done by telehealth.

Cancellations
We ask for at least 24 hours notice if you need to cancel or reschedule. Appointments missed or cancelled with less than 24 hours notice are subject to a $40 missed-appointment fee, which is not covered by insurance.

Billing
Most insurance plans cover one preventive physical per year at no cost to you. Additional services discussed or treated during the visit, such as a new problem or a chronic condition review, may be billed separately and may involve a copay. Questions about coverage should be directed to your insurance company; our billing office can provide the procedure codes.

Front desk hours: Monday to Friday, 7:30 a.m. to 6:00 p.m.; Saturday, 8:00 a.m. to 12:00 p.m.

FGEN-CTX-G3.title: Harbor & Pine customer experience team offsite - planning notes
FGEN-CTX-G3.text:
HARBOR & PINE - CUSTOMER EXPERIENCE TEAM OFFSITE

FGEN-CTX-I1.title: Sourdough starter feeding schedule
FGEN-CTX-I1.text:
SOURDOUGH STARTER - FEEDING SCHEDULE

Day 1: Mix 50 g whole wheat flour with 50 g lukewarm water in a clean jar. Cover loosely and leave at room temperature, ideally 24 to 26 C.

Day 2: You may see a few bubbles or nothing at all. Both are normal. Leave it alone.

Days 3 to 6: Once a day, discard all but 50 g of the starter, then add 50 g flour (half whole wheat, half white) and 50 g water. Stir well and mark the level on the jar with a rubber band.

Days 7 onward: Switch to two feedings a day, about 12 hours apart. A healthy starter should roughly double within 4 to 8 hours of feeding and smell pleasantly sour, like yogurt.

Troubleshooting
- Grey liquid on top ("hooch") means it is hungry. Pour it off and feed.
- No rise after day 10: move it somewhere warmer and use more whole wheat flour.
- Pink or orange streaks: throw it out and start again.

Storage
Once established, keep it in the fridge and feed once a week. Take it out the night before baking and give it two room-temperature feedings before mixing dough.

FLEC-CTX-G1.title: BIO 220 Lecture 15 slide notes: Kinase cascades and scaffolds
FLEC-CTX-G1.text:
BIO 220 - Cell Biology
Lecture 15: Signal amplification, kinase cascades, and scaffolds
Prof. Ingrid Achterberg. Slide notes.

1. Why cascades?
- Each active kinase can phosphorylate many copies of the next kinase, so a small input becomes a large output: amplification. Three tiers (MAPKKK to MAPKK to MAPK) is the textbook arrangement.
- Cascades can also produce switch-like (ultrasensitive) responses, where the output goes from low to high over a narrow range of input.
- Hill coefficient nH: nH = 1 is a graded response; nH > 1 is steeper. Course convention: call a response "switch-like" only if nH >= 2.

2. Scaffold proteins
- A scaffold binds several kinases of one cascade and holds them together.
- Three jobs we care about: speed (high local concentration), insulation (preventing cross-talk with other cascades that share a kinase), and regulation (the scaffold itself can be a control point).

3. Case study (slides 12-17): the Moravec lab handout
The numbers below come from the Moravec lab handout distributed in class, not from the textbook.
- Organism: budding yeast, pheromone response pathway. Scaffold protein: Pbr4 (course name).
- Strains: WT (wild type) and KY-17 (pbr4 deletion).
- Readout: fluorescent reporter, as % of maximum WT response, measured 60 minutes after pheromone is added.
- Dose-response: WT EC50 = 12 nM, Hill coefficient 2.6. KY-17 EC50 = 41 nM, Hill coefficient 1.1.
- Time to half-maximal response at saturating pheromone (100 nM): WT 9 min, KY-17 27 min.
- Maximum response at 100 nM: WT 100%, KY-17 88%.
- Cross-talk test: osmotic stress (0.4 M NaCl, no pheromone) activates the reporter to 3% in WT and 31% in KY-17.
- Replicates: n = 4 biological replicates per strain. The handout reports means only; no error bars or statistical tests were included.

4. How the prof wants you to read it
- "The knockout still signals. It is slower, less sensitive, graded instead of switch-like, and leaky to the wrong input. That is four phenotypes from one deletion."
- Lower sensitivity means a higher EC50. Every year students write that KY-17 is "more sensitive" because 41 is the bigger number. It is not.
- Loss of ultrasensitivity: nH falls from 2.6 to 1.1, so by the course convention KY-17 is no longer switch-like.
- Insulation: the jump from 3% to 31% under osmotic stress is the insulation phenotype.
- The handout does NOT establish mechanism for the slowdown. Two hypotheses were left open for discussion section: (a) reduced local concentration of the kinases, and (b) loss of an allosteric activation step that Pbr4 performs on the middle kinase.

5. Exam and assignment notes
- Problem Set 6, Q2: sketch both dose-response curves from the EC50 and Hill values. Put pheromone concentration in nM on a log-scale x-axis.
- Exam 3 will include one "read the data" question in this style, with a new table, not this one.
- Discussion section this week: come ready to argue for one of the two mechanism hypotheses using only the handout data.

FLEC-CTX-G2.title: STAT 301 Lecture 11 notes: Comparing two groups
FLEC-CTX-G2.text:
STAT 301 - Applied Statistics
Lecture 11: Comparing two groups
Prof. Renata Szabo. Lecture notes, course site copy.

1. Course conventions (apply to every test this term)
- Significance level: alpha = 0.01 for all in-class examples, problem sets and mini-projects, unless a question states otherwise. The prof's reason: "We run a lot of tests in this course, and I would rather you miss a small effect than chase noise."
- Two independent samples: use Welch's t-test by default. Do not assume equal variances unless a problem explicitly says the population variances are equal.
- Always report the test statistic, the degrees of freedom and the p-value, and state the conclusion in the context of the data, not as "reject H0" alone.
- Choose the test before looking at results. Switching tests after seeing a p-value is marked as an error on problem sets.

2. Paired vs independent designs
- Paired: the same unit measured twice (before and after, or two seasons on the same tree). Analyze the differences d = x1 - x2 with a one-sample t-test.
- Independent: two unrelated groups. Welch's t-test.
- Pairing helps most when the variation between units is large compared with the change within a unit, because taking differences cancels the unit-to-unit spread.
- Analyzing independent groups as if they were paired is invalid, not just less efficient.

3. Worked example: the Brennock Orchard data (slides 8-13)
- Question: do trees in the North plot yield more apples than trees in the South plot? Yield = kg of apples per tree, one harvest season.
- North plot: n = 14, mean 38.2 kg, SD 6.1 kg.
- South plot: n = 11, mean 31.5 kg, SD 9.8 kg.
- Welch's t-test: t = 1.99, df = 15.9, p = 0.065.
- For comparison only: a pooled-variance t-test on the same data gives t = 2.10, df = 23, p = 0.047. The prof showed this to make a point: "If you had picked pooled because the p-value looked nicer, you would be under 0.05 and you would have fooled yourself. Our rule is Welch, decided in advance."
- Frost week: three South trees were damaged in a late frost. With those three removed, South is n = 8, mean 35.9 kg, SD 5.4 kg, and Welch gives t = 0.92, df = 16.3, p = 0.37.
- Removing data points after seeing results has to be justified independently of the results. Here the justification is the orchard manager's frost log, dated before harvest.

4. Common mistakes flagged in lecture
- Reading p = 0.065 as "a 6.5% chance the plots are the same." It is not.
- Concluding "no difference" from a non-significant result. The correct wording is that the data do not provide convincing evidence of a difference at the chosen alpha.
- Reporting a confidence level that does not match alpha. With alpha = 0.01, report a 99% confidence interval.

5. Admin
- Problem Set 7 (two-sample tests) is due next Tuesday before lecture.
- Office hours this week: Thursday 1-3 pm, Math Annex 104.
- Mini-project 2 details were announced verbally in lecture; see the lecture recording.
