FJOB-CTX-G1.title: Portfolio case study: Saltmarsh offline field inspections
FJOB-CTX-G1.text:
PORTFOLIO CASE STUDY - SALTMARSH: OFFLINE-FIRST FIELD INSPECTIONS
My role: mobile and sync engineer (1 of 3 engineers). Timeline: April 2024 - January 2025.

THE PROBLEM
Ferrow County Water Authority sends inspectors out to check backflow valves, hydrants and meter vaults. Before Saltmarsh they filled in paper forms, then retyped them at the office. About a third of the sites have no cell signal at all, so an online-only app was never going to work. There were 42 inspectors when we started.

WHAT WE BUILT
- A React Native app (iOS and Android) that stores every inspection in SQLite on the device and works fully offline.
- A small Go sync service in front of PostgreSQL.
- A web dashboard for supervisors (built by my teammate Ines Carvalho; I only touched the export endpoint).

THE PART I OWNED: THE SYNC ENGINE
- Every record is split into fields, and each field carries its own version stamp: a hybrid logical clock value plus the device ID.
- When two inspectors edit the same inspection offline, the server merges field by field. If they changed different fields, both edits survive. If they changed the same field, the higher clock wins and the losing value is kept in a "conflict shelf" that the supervisor sees on the dashboard.
- Photos never conflict: they are append-only and keyed by a content hash, so a re-upload after a dropped connection is a no-op.
- Sync runs in batches of 50 records with a resumable cursor, so a sync that dies halfway through a canyon picks up where it stopped.
- In the first 6 months after launch, 214 field-level conflicts went to the conflict shelf. Supervisors overrode the automatic winner 9 times.

RESULTS
- Average time per inspection went from 26 minutes to 11 minutes (the county's own time study, 3 weeks before and 3 weeks after).
- Crash-free sessions went from 97.1% in the beta to 99.6% at the 1.0 release.
- Retyping at the office went away entirely; the county reassigned one clerk position to scheduling.

WHAT WENT WRONG
- In version 1.3 I shipped on-device photo compression to cut upload size. It worked, but it ran on the main thread at full resolution and drained batteries: inspectors reported phones dying by early afternoon. I rolled it back within 4 days, then moved compression to a background worker that only runs while charging. My lesson: I tested on a new phone plugged into my desk, not on a three-year-old phone in the field in August.
- I underestimated how long the Android permission flow for background location would take to get through review. We slipped the 1.0 date by two weeks.

WHAT I WOULD DO DIFFERENTLY
- Put a field test with real inspectors into every release, not just the big ones.
- Write the conflict rules down as a one-page spec earlier. We argued about "last writer wins" for weeks before agreeing on per-field clocks.

STACK
React Native, TypeScript, SQLite (op-sqlite), Go, PostgreSQL, Sentry, GitHub Actions, Fastlane.

MY ANGLE

Req QH-0417: Staff Data Engineer, Claims Analytics

Level: Staff (IC6). Base salary band: $205,000 to $238,000. Target annual bonus: 10% of base, paid in February based on company and individual performance. Equity: RSUs with a 4-year vest; amounts are discussed only at offer stage. Recruiters should not quote an equity number.

This req cannot provide any visa sponsorship, including transfers. Candidates must be authorized to work in the US without sponsorship now and in the future.

Business-hours on-call only, one week in six. No overnight paging; failed overnight loads are handled the next morning.

1. Recruiter screen (30 min)

3. Loop, split across two days:
   - SQL and data modeling, live (75 min)
   - Pipeline design (60 min)

- Own the claims warehouse data model and cut the nightly build from about 7 hours to under 3.
- Replace the legacy Spark jobs with dbt models.
- Establish data contracts with the ingestion team for late-arriving claims and adjustments.

Must-haves
Deep SQL and dimensional modeling, production experience with Snowflake or a comparable warehouse, handling late-arriving and restated data, and the ability to explain tradeoffs to non-engineers.

Nice to have
Healthcare claims experience (837 and 835 formats), actuarial partnerships, dbt at scale.

FSEM-CTX-G1.title: Thesis chapter 5 - battery capacity fade in a shared e-bike fleet
FSEM-CTX-G1.text:
Ph.D. thesis draft, School of Electrical and Energy Engineering, Castleford Institute
Chapter 5 - Battery capacity fade in the Portmere shared e-bike fleet

5.1 Data
The operator shared battery management system (BMS) telemetry for all 1,140 bikes in the Portmere fleet from October 2021 to November 2023 (26 months). Every bike uses the same pack model, the LX-36 (36 V, 14 Ah). Remaining capacity was estimated monthly from the BMS state-of-health field. Usage is expressed as equivalent full cycles.

97 packs running BMS firmware 2.x were excluded because that firmware misreported state of health after partial charges. The analysis therefore uses 1,043 packs.

5.2 Charging temperature rather than depot
Packs are charged overnight at one of three depots. Depot B is unheated; depots A and C are heated. Because the operator rebalanced bikes between depots almost every week, a pack's depot was not stable over time. Instead of depot, each pack was characterised by its median charging temperature, taken from the cell temperature sensor at the start of each charge.

5.3 Model
A linear mixed model of capacity against equivalent full cycles, with a random slope for each pack. Candidate predictors of the fade rate were median charging temperature, share of fast charges (above 1C), and share of trips that ended below 10% state of charge.

5.4 Results
The median fade rate across the fleet was 2.1% of original capacity per 100 equivalent full cycles.

Charging temperature was the strongest predictor. Packs whose median charging temperature was below 5 degrees C faded at 3.3% per 100 cycles, compared with 1.9% per 100 cycles for packs whose median charging temperature was above 15 degrees C.

Once charging temperature was in the model, the share of fast charges had no significant effect on fade rate (p = 0.31). In a model without temperature, fast charging did appear significant, because fast chargers were concentrated at depot B.

Packs that regularly ended trips below 10% state of charge faded 0.4 percentage points faster per 100 cycles than packs that rarely did.

By the end of the study, 212 of the 1,043 analysed packs (20.3%) had fallen below the operator's end-of-life threshold of 80% of original capacity.

5.5 Implications
The results support moving winter charging out of depot B and into heated depots. The operator began a trial of this in January 2024. Its effect is outside the period of this chapter and has not been analysed. No cost or savings estimate was made in this chapter.

5.6 Limitations
- Capacity comes from BMS estimates, not from bench discharge tests or teardown of packs.
- Internal resistance was not measured.
- Only one pack model (LX-36) and one city's climate.
- Cell temperature at the start of charging is a proxy for charging conditions; temperature during the whole charge was not logged.
- Excluding the firmware 2.x packs may bias results if those packs were used differently; their usage pattern was not compared.

FSEM-CTX-G2.title: Seminar slides - review wait time and escaped defects
FSEM-CTX-G2.text:
Seminar slides - Does waiting for review let more bugs escape? Evidence from Quillon Labs
Software Engineering Research Seminar

Slide 1 - Question
Is a longer wait for the first code review associated with more defects escaping to production?

Slide 2 - Setting and data
- Quillon Labs (fictional mid-sized software company), 14 repositories.
- 3,812 merged pull requests, January to December 2023.
- Time to first review (TTFR): hours from PR opened to first reviewer comment or approval.
- Escaped defect: a bug ticket linked to the PR within 60 days of release.

Slide 3 - Descriptives
- Median TTFR: 5.6 hours.
- 11% of PRs waited more than 24 hours for first review.

Slide 4 - Raw comparison
- TTFR under 4 hours: escaped-defect rate 3.1%.
- TTFR over 24 hours: escaped-defect rate 6.8%.

Slide 5 - Adjusted model
Logistic regression adjusting for PR size (lines changed), author tenure and repository.
- TTFR over 24 h vs under 4 h: odds ratio 1.42 (95% CI 1.08 to 1.87).
- PR size over 400 lines vs under 100 lines: odds ratio 2.3.
- PR size is the strongest single predictor.

Slide 6 - Why might delay matter?
- Reviews that start after 24 hours leave fewer comments (median 2 comments vs 4 for reviews within 4 hours).
- Our reading: context loss and rubber-stamping of stale PRs. This is a hypothesis; review quality was not measured directly.

Slide 7 - How good is the defect linkage?
- Linking a bug ticket to a PR depends on engineers tagging it.
- Audit of 200 tickets: 22% of bug tickets had no PR link.
- If unlinked bugs are spread evenly across PRs, the odds ratio is unaffected; if they cluster in slow-review PRs, we underestimate the effect.

Slide 8 - Limitations
- Observational: teams with slow reviews may differ in other ways.
- One company.
- No measure of reviewer experience or seniority.
- Every PR in the data had at least one reviewer; the number of reviewers per PR was not recorded.
- Developer satisfaction and cost were not measured.

Slide 9 - Conclusion
Long waits for first review are associated with more escaped defects even after adjusting for PR size, but PR size matters more.

Slide 10 - Next step
A pilot of a 4-hour first-review target in two repositories has been proposed to engineering leadership. It has not yet run.

FSEM-CTX-C1.title: Draft 3 extended abstract - sleep coaching for night-shift nurses
FSEM-CTX-C1.text:
Extended abstract (Draft 3) - Sleep hygiene coaching for night-shift nurses
Nursing and Health Sciences Research Seminar

Abstract
In a randomized controlled trial with 96 nurses working permanent night shifts at Brenmoor General Hospital, a six-session sleep hygiene coaching programme increased sleep duration by 48 minutes per day at 8 weeks compared with usual care. Coaching covered light exposure, caffeine timing, and a fixed pre-sleep routine.

Methods
88 nurses enrolled across 6 wards. Allocation was by ward: 3 wards were allocated to coaching and 3 to usual care, so all nurses on the same ward received the same condition. Coaching was delivered by a trained occupational health nurse in six fortnightly sessions. The primary outcome was sleep duration measured by self-report sleep diary, recorded for one week at baseline and one week at the 12-week follow-up. A subset of 30 nurses also wore wrist actigraphs.

Results
Of the nurses enrolled, 79 completed follow-up. Mean sleep duration increased by 34 minutes (SD 41) in the coaching wards and by 6 minutes (SD 38) in usual-care wards. Nurses in coaching wards also reported lower daytime sleepiness. Actigraphy results for the subset are still being processed.

Discussion
Coaching appears to lengthen daytime sleep for night-shift nurses. Because allocation was by ward, ward culture and staffing levels could partly explain differences between groups; the analysis did not yet account for clustering by ward. Two coaching-ward nurses and seven usual-care nurses were lost to follow-up, mostly because of transfers to day shifts. The coaching programme took about six hours of each nurse's time in total and was scheduled during paid shifts. A larger trial across three hospitals is being planned.
FSEM-CTX-C1.notes: Contradictions: abstract says 96 nurses vs 88 enrolled in methods (79 completed); abstract says randomized controlled trial but methods describe allocation by ward (cluster, randomization not stated); abstract claims +48 minutes vs results +34 minutes (SD 41) in coaching wards; abstract follow-up at 8 weeks vs 12-week follow-up in methods; abstract implies an objective effect but the primary outcome is self-report diary and actigraphy is unprocessed; abstract does not mention the unadjusted ward clustering.

FTECH-CTX-G1.title: Candidate's take-home write-up: etcd cluster debug (Nimbuscrest)
FTECH-CTX-G1.text:
TAKE-HOME WRITE-UP: FLEET RELIABILITY CLUSTER DEBUG
Candidate: Dashiell Marrow | Submitted to Nimbuscrest Cloud | Time used: 84 of 90 minutes

Environment as given
Three control-plane nodes (fr-cp-1, fr-cp-2, fr-cp-3), Kubernetes 1.30 with stacked etcd 3.5 on each node. Each node has local NVMe and a shared volume mounted at /mnt/shared.

Symptoms
- kubectl calls failed intermittently with "etcdserver: request timed out".
- etcd logged 14 leader elections in the first 20 minutes I watched.
- API server latency for LIST calls jumped from about 80 ms to several seconds during each election.

Step 1: clocks
chronyc tracking on fr-cp-3 showed an offset of 1.8 s from the other two nodes. I corrected it by restarting chronyd against the internal NTP pool. The election rate did not change (13 elections in the next 20 minutes), so I recorded the skew as a secondary finding, not the root cause. Raft elections in etcd are driven by heartbeat and election timeouts measured locally, not by wall-clock agreement between nodes.

Step 2: disk
I pulled etcd_disk_wal_fsync_duration_seconds from each member. p99 on fr-cp-1 was 480 ms; on fr-cp-2 and fr-cp-3 it was 6 ms. The etcd guidance we follow wants WAL fsync p99 under 10 ms. On fr-cp-1, /var/lib/etcd was a symlink into /mnt/shared, which is an NFS export. Every time fr-cp-1 was leader it stalled on fsync, missed heartbeats (heartbeat-interval 100 ms, election-timeout 1000 ms), and the followers started a new election.

Step 3: fix
I removed fr-cp-1 from the cluster with etcdctl member remove, wiped its data directory, pointed it at /var/lib/etcd on local NVMe, and added it back with etcdctl member add. It then caught up from the leader's snapshot. I chose remove and re-add over copying the files because a copy would have carried over a WAL written during the fsync stalls, and the member had to go down either way. During the change the cluster ran on the two healthy members, so writes continued, but it could not have survived another failure until fr-cp-1 caught up.

Result: fsync p99 on fr-cp-1 dropped to 7 ms, and there were 0 leader elections in the following 60 minutes of observation.

Step 4: certificates
While checking member health I noticed the peer TLS certificate on fr-cp-2 expires on 2026-10-03. I renewed it with kubeadm certs renew etcd-peer and restarted that member. This was not causing the outage but would have caused one.

Not finished
- I wrote a Prometheus alert for WAL fsync p99 above 25 ms for 10 minutes, but did not have time to test that it fires.
- I did not check whether other workloads also write to /mnt/shared from fr-cp-1.

What I would monitor
- WAL fsync and backend commit durations per member.
- Leader changes per hour, alerting above 3.
- Certificate expiry, alerting 30 days out.

FTECH-CTX-G2.title: Tallowmarket Partner Payouts API v0.3 draft (design exercise)
FTECH-CTX-G2.text:
TALLOWMARKET PARTNER PAYOUTS API - v0.3 DRAFT
Owner: Payments & Ledger | Status: draft for interview design exercise

Overview
Partners (logistics co-ops that aggregate many growers) use this API to request payouts to growers once deliveries are confirmed. All amounts are integers in minor units. v0.3 supports USD only.

Authentication
OAuth 2.0 client credentials. Tokens last 60 minutes. Every request must carry a bearer token scoped to payouts:write or payouts:read.

POST /v1/payouts
Creates a payout request.
Body fields:
- grower_id (string, required)
- amount_minor (integer, required, 1 to 25,000,000)
- currency (string, required, must be "USD")
- order_ids (array of strings, 1 to 50 items)
- memo (string, optional, up to 140 characters)
Headers:
- Idempotency-Key (required, UUID v4)

Idempotency rules
- Keys are retained for 24 hours after the first request that used them.
- Same key and identical body: the original response is returned again with the header Idempotent-Replayed: true. No second payout is created.
- Same key and a different body: 422 with error code idempotency_key_reused.
- Same key while the first request is still being processed: 409 with error code request_in_progress. The client should retry after a short delay.

Payout statuses
pending -> held -> released, or pending -> held -> reversed.
- pending: accepted, not yet funded from escrow.
- held: funds reserved in escrow.
- released: sent in the nightly settlement batch.
- reversed: cancelled while held. Once released, a payout cannot be reversed through this API.

POST /v1/payouts/{id}/reverse
Allowed only while status is held. Returns 409 with error code not_reversible otherwise.

GET /v1/payouts/{id}
Returns the payout and its status history with timestamps.

Rate limits
50 requests per second per partner, with bursts up to 100. Over the limit the API returns 429 with a Retry-After header in seconds.

Webhooks
Events: payout.released and payout.reversed. Delivery is at-least-once; each event carries an event_id that partners should use to deduplicate. Failed deliveries (any non-2xx or no response within 10 seconds) are retried up to 8 times with exponential backoff over about 24 hours. Payloads are signed with HMAC-SHA256 in the Tallow-Signature header.

Errors
Errors return JSON with code, message and request_id. Error codes are stable; messages may change.

Out of scope for v0.3
Refunds, chargebacks, multi-currency payouts, and payout scheduling. These will be designed separately.

Open questions for the exercise
- How should the idempotency store be built so the 409 and 422 cases behave correctly under concurrent retries?
- Should GET support listing payouts by grower with cursor pagination?

FTECH-CTX-C1.title: Fleet Reliability take-home brief (errata merged)
FTECH-CTX-C1.text:
NIMBUSCREST CLOUD - FLEET RELIABILITY TAKE-HOME (candidate copy, errata merged)

Overview
You will receive SSH access to a three-node Kubernetes control plane (fr-cp-1, fr-cp-2, fr-cp-3) whose etcd cluster is unhealthy. Your job is to find what is wrong, fix it, and write up what you did. You have 90 minutes from the moment you first log in.

Environment
- Kubernetes 1.30, stacked etcd 3.5 on each control-plane node.
- Each node has a local NVMe disk and a shared volume mounted at /mnt/shared.
- Once you are done, the cluster must be able to tolerate the loss of two members.

Rules
- Do not restart etcd members; we want to see how you diagnose without disruption.
- You may use any tools already installed. Do not install packages from the internet.
- Keep a timestamped log of the commands you run.

What to submit
- A write-up of no more than two pages: symptoms, root cause, fix, and what you would monitor.
- Your command log.

ERRATA (added after the brief was first sent)
- E1: The environment now has five control-plane nodes (fr-cp-1 through fr-cp-5). Ignore the node count above.
- E2: The etcd version is 3.4.27, not 3.5.
- E3: You have 2 hours. The timer starts when the environment is provisioned, not at first login.
- E4: You may restart any member if you explain why in the write-up.

Grading
We look at the order in which you ruled things out, not only at whether you found everything. Partial solutions with a clear write-up are fine.
